question.text: What is STE-80, and how does writing to it make a technical sentence easier to read?
question.known_at: Captions 1–2 ("This is STE-80… It uses about eighty percent of the rules of ASD-STE100"). The 'how' becomes clear at caption 6 ("Here is a typical sentence").
question.result_stated: Partly: "Sixteen words became nine. The reader still fills the reservoir before starting the machine, with less work to read it." What STE-80 consists of, compared with full STE, is never stated.

reply.motive: Reason to care: "Manuals are read under time pressure, often in a second language, so every word must help." This is tied to aircraft manuals and not to the viewer's own technical writing. Reason for the approach (why use 80% of the rules and not all of them): missing.
reply.close: Partly. "Sixteen words became nine… with less work to read it" answers the demo. The ending then turns to "Full STE has more rules" without saying what STE-80 is in general, and does not return to "every word must help".
reply.recap: STE-80 is a lighter form of Simplified Technical English. It uses simple words, direct instructions and concrete verbs, and here it cut a 16-word manual sentence to 9 words.
reply.strongest: Captions 6–7 together with the running word-count bar: "It has sixteen words: the orange bar counts them." It gives a clear, measurable thread that runs through the whole video.
reply.weakest: Captions 23–24: "Full STE has more rules…". The ending is ambiguous, adds new material, and never says how STE-80 relates to these rules.
suggestions: Say once which rules STE-80 keeps and which it drops (for example, whether it skips the approved dictionary). Make the ending an explicit contrast.
Expand ASD and say directly that STE is short for Simplified Technical English.
In caption 13, signal the quote in speech, e.g. 'Cut the phrase "it is imperative that the operator ensures"', and drop "frame".
Fix caption 8 "The words in red go" to "The words in red change".
Give a reason for each rule (who acts, one action per step, no abstract nouns). Admit or fix the meaning shifts from "make sure" to "fill" and from "operation" to "machine".
Make the faint text on screen readable, or say it out loud.
